paras: The whitecapping of Robinson's farm near Johnson Station was a night raid in late September or early October 1903 in which whitecappers destroyed the fences and crops of Robinson, a Black landowner in Lincoln County, Mississippi. The same report said that Jim Williams, a Black man living just across the county line in Pike County, had his property treated in the same way. The Brookhaven Leader, which learned of the raid secondhand, treated it as 'another case' of whitecapping and condemned it as 'a disgrace to civilization'.

Robinson's farm lay two miles west of Johnson Station, on the line between Lincoln and Pike counties in southern Mississippi. The Leader noted that Robinson 'owned his own place in Lincoln' and called the raid 'another case of whitecapping'.

According to the Leader, a 'squad of whitecappers' visited Robinson's farm on 'last Friday night' before its 3 October issue. The raiders tore down all of his fencing, beat out the open cotton in his field, scattered several hundred pounds of cotton he had already picked over the ground, and pulled and partly destroyed his standing corn. Jim Williams, living just across the line in Pike County, was also visited and his property 'similarly treated, so the report goes'. No injuries were reported, and the raiders were not named.

The Leader could not obtain full particulars; its information came from white citizens of that part of the county who did not want their names used. No report of arrests or a prosecution appears in the coverage.

Only white Mississippi papers reported the raid; no Black-press account was found. The Brookhaven Leader carried the original item on 3 October 1903 under the headline 'Whitecapping in South Lincoln', and closed it with an editorial line that such acts of 'vandalism, whether committed on white or black', deserved 'the severest punishment and condemnation'. On 8 October the Brandon News reprinted the news almost word for word as 'Two New Cases of White Capping Reported', changing 'last Friday night' to 'one night recently' and omitting the condemnation.

accounts.gist: White citizens from the area, who did not want their names used, told the Leader in Brookhaven that whitecappers had wrecked Robinson's fences and crops and treated Williams's property the same way; the paper could not obtain full particulars.

framing.detail: Headlined 'Whitecapping in South Lincoln', the Leader called such acts 'vandalism' and 'a disgrace to civilization' that should be met with 'the severest punishment and condemnation', whether done to white or Black.
The Brandon News ran the news paragraphs as 'Two New Cases of White Capping Reported' under 'Late News Mississippi', without the Leader's editorial comment.

Later whitecapping in southwestern Lincoln: Eli Hilson's house shot into, Henry List killed; separate episode.
